#10138. A Chinese bottle-cap manufacturer brilliantly deflated AI hype

Pre-digital tech can't be transformed and automated

Shanghai is one of the world’s largest and busiest cities but is surprisingly quiet. Electric automobiles cruise silently, chased by hushed flocks of electric scooters.

When I visited in early November to attend the local edition of the AI Engineer conference, I found China's attitude to AI is also quite relaxed. That's not to say interest in the topic is low, but I didn't perceive any anxious artificial-general-intelligence-is-coming-and-will-destroy-us vibe.

The only conference talk that referenced AGI came from Ying Yang, a neuroscience PhD and serious influencer who has over 3.4 million followers on Chinese micro-blogging service Weibo, who enthused about the marketing and product development opportunities opening up to those who prepare for what’s coming.

AGI isn't P(doom) for the Chinese AI practitioners I met; it's a great new marketing tool.

Some of this may be due to the fact that the major US model makers like OpenAI, Anthropic and Google are effectively inaccessible on the Chinese side of the Great Firewall.

Engineers in China use DeepSeek or Kimi or GLM or MiniMax or MiMo or Qwen, all of which are now more than good enough for almost any task, and all offered without reference to The Terminator.

That's not to say that Chinese engineers and designers aren't facing the same crisis of self-worth we've seen elsewhere. A spectacular keynote from Ryo Lu asked, "When we can do anything, do we still know what we want?" Are our measures of self-worth pointless when we can no longer prove who we are by how many lines of code we've written, or frameworks we've designed?

Ryo landed on a line I'm hearing more frequently: "I want to build tools to help me be more and more involved, not prove that I'm needed less and less."

What followed showed just how good that tooling has become and what an AI engineer can do with it.

I saw an impressive demo from AutoArk of a 35 billion-parameter model running in just 2.5GB of smartphone RAM on an iPhone 16 Pro. DYNA's Zhong Shen showed how it builds robot hardware that will work with AI models updating every month.

My favorite presentation came from a bottle cap manufacturer called named Zhu Shihui, who reminded everyone in the audience that “the last mile is half the journey.”

Zhu flayed the class of consultants who never realize some manufacturing equipment is pre-digital but still insist every process can be easily automated. Never mind that workers in those factories lack deep digital skills (Zhu's average employee is in their late 40s) and that companies of this sort operate on margins so thin that resources simply aren't available to mount a complete transformation. Instead of swinging in on an AI wrecking ball, Zhu suggested the best approach is to exercise humility by seeking out an organization's tacit knowledge and using that as the basis for transformation.

Not long after Zhu left the podium, one of my Australian fellow travelers noted the significant proportion of women at the conference. I hadn't noticed, because having equal numbers of men and women at an engineering conference felt perfectly normal. Yet it's not something I've ever experienced at AI events in Australia or America. Whatever else the Chinese are doing with AI, they've put gender politics aside in AI engineering.

To put that in context: not long after leaving Shanghai, Alice Huang became major global news. A Shanghainese woman working in AI might look suspicious to an American who only ever sees men working in the field. Fei-Fei Li, Mira Murati and Daniela Amodei stand out as exceptions that prove the rule, but none of them, despite stellar work, have anywhere near the profiles of their male peers. In China, it's different.

It's become commonplace to be dismissive of Chinese progress in AI, ascribing it to copying, "distillation" and outright theft. Yet the Chinese make both the best small models and the best robots, and are moving ever-closer to making them work well together.

Chinese labs share their results with their peers and their competitors: nearly every model, closed or open, has benefited from the research done by DeepSeek and Alibaba. Practicality, balance and openness seem to be serving them well. Perhaps, after OpenAI follows Anthropic out to the public markets, and shareholders get a voice, stability, sanity and a bit of quiet will cross the Pacific. Those are some Chinese imports I'm looking forward to. ®

#10137. AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

HeadlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough shows a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions.

Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data.

How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. #10136. Model Routing Is Simple. Until It Isn’t.

Building a router into your agent sounds like an easy win. Send simple requests to cheaper models, reserve expensive ones for harder tasks, or route by specialty — Claude for code, Gemini for multimodal, and so on. A classifier or heuristic makes the call, costs go down, performance stays up. Done.

Except it’s not. Most routing systems assume that model selection is a classification problem. In our experience building routing into agentic systems, what looks like a model-selection problem quickly becomes a systems optimization problem. Three dimensions made this surprisingly hard for us.

We expected GPT-4.1 to be cheaper than Claude Sonnet 4.6. It wasn’t.

Across 417 tasks on the AppWorld Test Challenge using the same CodeAct agent, Sonnet cost $79 total ($0.19/task) while GPT-4.1 cost $155 ($0.37/task) — nearly double. On paper, this makes no sense. GPT-4.1’s token pricing is lower on both input and output, and Sonnet takes roughly three times as many reasoning steps to finish the same tasks. By sticker price alone, GPT-4.1 should win easily.

The explanation? Caching — something most routing discussions ignore entirely. Agent workloads tend to reuse large chunks of context across steps. When cache hit rates are high, effective input costs drop dramatically. Sonnet’s lower cache-read pricing meant it benefited disproportionately from this pattern, enough to overcome both its higher base pricing and its longer trajectories.

The takeaway: actual cost depends on the interaction between the model, the workload, and the serving infrastructure. A router that only looks at pricing sheets is optimizing against the wrong numbers.

A common routing strategy is to estimate how hard a task is and send harder tasks to stronger models. Intuitive, but it breaks down in two ways.

First, difficulty is often invisible at routing time. A request like "summarize this contract" looks simple, but might trigger retrieval, compliance checks, tool use, and multiple rounds of refinement before it’s done. Meanwhile, a highly technical prompt might be handled efficiently by a smaller specialized model. You often don’t know how hard a task actually is until execution is underway.

Routers aren’t solving one problem. They’re constantly juggling cost, quality, latency, compliance, and reliability all at once.

It’s tempting to think about latency purely in terms of model size — bigger models are slower, smaller ones are faster. But what the user actually experiences depends on much more than that.

Routing itself adds overhead. Infrastructure factors — which hardware a model is running on, whether the cache is warm, how busy the endpoint is — often dominate end-to-end response times. A theoretically faster model can still produce a slower experience if the serving conditions aren’t right.

Then there’s routing granularity. Routing once per task adds minimal overhead. But routing at every step — which gives you more flexibility to adapt mid-execution — means every additional decision point introduces latency and operational complexity.

A router that ignores the serving system is optimizing against the wrong reality.

These lessons shaped how we built our router. The key shift: we stopped treating routing as a classification problem and started treating it as an optimization problem. Rather than asking "which model is best for this task?", our algorithm optimizes across cost, quality, and latency simultaneously — while staying lightweight enough to avoid becoming a bottleneck itself.

The figure below shows the result on the AppWorld Test Challenge with a CodeAct agent. Each blue square is a different configuration of our router, tracing out a cost-accuracy frontier. The important thing isn't any single point — it's that the router gives you a range of operating points to choose from depending on whether you want to prioritize cost, latency, or accuracy. Configuration 1 (latency-optimized) lands at 84% accuracy for $93 and 83s — a 21% cost reduction and 9% latency reduction compared to running Opus alone, with only a 4% accuracy drop. Configuration 2 pushes cost even lower.

Notice that a standard difficulty-based router (the teal diamond) lands in a similar accuracy range but at higher cost — it doesn't explore the full tradeoff space the way an optimization-based approach can. And because the optimization itself is lightweight (roughly 6 ms and 2 kB of memory per task), the router doesn't become the bottleneck we warned about earlier.

The lesson we took away from this work is that routing isn’t really about choosing models. It’s about optimizing systems. Models are one variable — an important one, but just one among caching behavior, infrastructure state, compliance constraints, and workload patterns.

When routing works well, it’s rarely because it found the "best" model for a given task. It’s because it found the best operating point for the entire system. That’s a harder problem than classification, but it’s the one worth solving.

We’ll be sharing more about the technical details behind our approach in a follow-up post. In the meantime, if you’re building routing into your own agentic systems, we’d love to hear what tradeoffs you’re running into.

This post was influenced by numerous conversations with colleagues, whose thoughtful questions, feedback, and insights helped refine our thinking.

So I've always felt that model routing is a false proposition; it should have been part of the harness all along.

Agreed, routing should disappear into the harness and just be part of the system's execution logic. Our goal is exactly that—making model choice an intrinsic capability rather than a separate concern.

#10134. Time for frustrated M365 customers to stage a 'distributed denial of satisfaction' action

Microsoft is asking customers to apply for reimbursement. They should protest

I briefly helped with Microsoft Australia’s PR efforts in the early 2000s, when IE 6 and Windows were so bug-prone they essentially represented a welcome mat for hackers and required a deluge of patches admins couldn’t handle. Microsoft responded to that mess with a message about security being a shared responsibility involving people, process, and technology.

A quarter of a century later, Microsoft’s business practices still make its customers reluctantly share the cost of its failings – most recently last week’s massive M365 outage.

To protest that mess, Microsoft customers should create a new cloudy meltdown – on the pages the software giant uses to process applications for compensation after it fails to meet service level agreements.

Yes, you read that right: “applications.” When Microsoft experiences an outage, customers must apply to get the service credits they’re entitled by finding the “Outage ID” related to each incident. The application page is buried deep in the Microsoft 365 Admin Center and the Outage ID is recorded elsewhere. Microsoft appears not to offer a facility for bulk uploads, so the channel partners who manage so many M365 implementations have extra work to do.

That’s outrageous because the implicit promise of the cloud is that it delivers more value for less effort. Yet Microsoft requires users to do extra work to seek redress for its mistakes.

Cloud also delivers fat profits for investors. Which is probably why Microsoft, which can clearly bill its customers regularly and reliably and therefore knows which services they use, hasn’t done the work to link its uptime meters and billing systems so it can automate crediting customers after outages.

I understand Microsoft thinks AI is quite good at that sort of integration. Maybe its enormously reduced workforce will need it to get the job done.

But rather than vibe-coding its way out of this, decency demands Microsoft quickly decide that all users impacted by last week’s automatically receive service credits, rather than asking them apply for their entitlements.

If Microsoft doesn’t get proactive, the magnitude of this outage represents a moment in which its customers can show the software giant it must do better – perhaps by filing so many applications for credit that managers who oversee Redmond’s systems and finances can’t help but notice a spike of activity.

Thinks of this as a distributed denial of satisfaction attack signaling that Microsoft can't solve this particular outage with a glib apology and a blog post. ®

#10133. Security incident disclosure — July 2026

Earlier this week, we detected and responded to an intrusion into part of our production infrastructure. This one was different from anything we had handled before in one important way: it was driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system - and we detected and dissected it largely with AI of our own.

We identified unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and to several credentials used by our services. We are still completing our assessment of whether any partner or customer data was affected, and we will contact any affected parties directly as required. We have found no evidence of tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and our software supply chain (container images and published packages) was verified clean.

The intrusion started where AI platforms are uniquely exposed: the data-processing pipeline. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths in our dataset processing (a remote-code dataset loader and a template-injection in a dataset configuration) to run code on a processing worker. From there, the actor escalated to node-level access, harvested cloud and cluster credentials, and moved laterally into several internal clusters over a weekend.

The campaign was run by an autonomous agent framework (appearing to be built on an agentic security-research harness - used LLM still not known) executing many thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes, with self-migrating command-and-control staged on public services. This matches the "agentic attacker" scenario the industry has been forecasting.

We are working with outside cybersecurity forensic specialists to investigate the issue and review our security policies and procedures. Finally, we have also reported this incident to law enforcement agencies.

As a precaution, we recommend rotating any access tokens and reviewing recent activity on your account. If you believe you are affected, or want to report a security concern, contact us at security@huggingface.co.

We are grateful to the teams across Hugging Face who responded around the clock, and we are sorry for any disruption this caused. Security is never finished; we will keep raising the bar.

The attack was initially surfaced through AI-assisted detection. Our anomaly-detection pipeline uses LLM-based triage over security telemetry to separate real signals from the daily noise, and it was the correlation of those signals that flagged the compromise.

To understand what a swarm of tens of thousands of automated actions did, we ran LLM-driven analysis agents over the full attacker action log, comprised of more than 17,000 recorded events. This allowed us to reconstruct the timeline, extract indicators of compromise, map the credentials touched, and separate genuine impact from decoy activity. Thanks to this approach, we were able to do in hours what would usually take days, and match the adversary's speed.

The choice of models we could use for this analysis was constrained in a way we did not anticipate; we describe this below.

When we started the log analysis, we first used frontier models behind commercial APIs. This did not work: the analysis requires submitting large volumes of real attack commands, exploit payloads, and C2 artifacts, and these requests were blocked by the providers' safety guardrails, which cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker. We ran the forensic analysis instead on zai-org/GLM-5.2, an open-weight model, on our own infrastructure. This had a second benefit: no attacker data, and none of the credentials it referenced, left our environment.

This experience points to a gap worth planning for. We do not know which model powered the attacker's agents, whether a jailbroken hosted model or an unrestricted open-weight one; either way, the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried. The practical lesson for defenders: have a capable model you can run on your own infrastructure vetted and ready before an incident, both to avoid guardrail lockout and to keep attacker data and credentials from leaving your environment. This is not an argument against safety measures on hosted models, and we are sharing this feedback with the providers concerned.

Autonomous, AI-driven offensive tooling is no longer theoretical. It lowers the cost of running a broad, patient, multi-stage campaign, and it operates at machine speed. Defending an online platform now means treating the data and model surface as a first-class attack surface, and using AI on defense to keep pace. We will keep investing there, and keep sharing what we learn.

#10132. Artex: The AI Pen-Test Tool Hackers Turned Into a Weapon

Forks of the open source Artex framework, along with 45 similar pen-testing tools, remain capable of executing credential attacks and cloud breaches at machine speed across multiple industries.

AI penetration-testing tool Artex has proven to be a boon for threat actors large and small, taking familiar attacker playbooks and deploying them at machine speeds — ushering in a potentially new era for defenders looking to get ahead of AI-enabled threats.

In July, independent developer Autumn-27 published Artex to GitHub, an open source, multiagent AI penetration testing framework written in Go. It is, by intention, a legitimate tool. However, as is so often the case with pen-test tools (such as, famously, Cobalt Strike), threat actors found a way to take advantage of it for malicious use. By late summer and early fall, a range of threat actors were using it as part of their toolkit.

Artex is capable of brute-forcing passwords, dumping databases, enumerating and abusing APIs, and more. This positions it for credential compromise and lateral movement in its own right, but the agentic element means Artex can operate at inhuman speeds. Microsoft saw an AI agent move from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from an Azure Key Vault in five minutes, for example.

Related:Russia's Cold Relic APT Turns One Cloud Breach Into Another

Steve Winterfeld, advisory CISO for Akamai, tells Dark Reading that while legitimate tool misuse is a known quantity, AI reduces the effort and expertise required to execute complex attacks. "What is particularly noteworthy about the Artex campaigns is the acceleration in speed, coordination, and autonomy," he says. "Activities that previously required deliberate integration can now be chained together and executed with limited hacking skills."

At the end of October, Artex's creator deleted the original GitHub repository due to rampant abuse, but many forks of the tool remain, so the threat remains. But even if all the forks went offline and Artex was no longer a going concern, the underlying threat of frameworks like it is far from over.

GitGuardian yesterday, for instance, detailed 45 different agentic attack frameworks (Artex "siblings" as the researchers called them) that are all capable of conducting attacks autonomously with the help of an AI model. Depending on the tool, these pen-testing frameworks are capable of end-to-end attacks against a network, Web application targeting, and/or autonomous coding. Some even include built-in command-and-control functionality. That's not to say these tools are inherently bad — pen-testing tools have many legitimate use cases — but it does illustrate the wide range of options for today's attacker.

The best-known incident to date involved China's Storm-0940, which adapted Artex source code into its own offensive infrastructure. Last month, around Oct. 10, the actor used the Artex framework to launch a massive password-spraying and credential-stuffing campaign against more than 300 specific user accounts at eight critical organizations, making more than 151,000 authentication requests in the process. On average, this represented 2,900 attempts per minute without triggering automated lockout or alert.

Related:China-Nexus Actors Breach 10 Organizations in AI-Driven Attacks

When this largely failed, Storm-0940 pivoted to target ConnectWise's internal infrastructure. Attackers exfiltrated trusted OAuth application credentials belonging to ConnectWise's Cloud Backup application, allowing them to compromise more than 2,250 downstream Microsoft 365 and Azure environments within three hours of initial targeting.

Abuse extends far beyond a single threat actor or objective. Microsoft last week published a blog post discussing how a financially motivated Cambodia-based threat cluster tracked as Storm-3358 started using Artex in its attacks against financial organizations primarily (but not exclusively) in Southeast Asia. Microsoft said it observed Storm-3358 using Artex in combination with conventional automated tools to scan systems connected to the public Internet, exploit vulnerabilities, and install open source remote access Trojans (RATs).

Related:Inside an AI Attack Against a US Retailer

Microsoft added that other threat actors have used Artex agents "to scan and exploit vulnerabilities in Web applications, use Web shells for persistence on compromised Web servers, compromise credentials from public sources and compromised systems, and use compromised cloud identities for persistence and data exfiltration."

CrowdStrike on Oct. 29 connected Artex-powered espionage activity to a threat actor it tracks as Vapor Panda, India's CERT (CERT-In) tracked a financially motivated threat actor hitting financial institutions, and as of Nov. 4, Censys observed more than 1,400 internet-exposed Artex console deployments. That said, because Internet exposure is not required for use, Censys estimated actual global use to be higher.

Recent Artex activity stands out because much of the story involves things security practitioners have seen time and time again. Pen-test tool abuse, nation-state tooling moving downstream to financially motivated attackers, password spraying, supply chain attacks, AI — it's a threat intelligence greatest hits album. But Guillaume Valadon, head of cybersecurity research at GitGuardian, tells Dark Reading what stands out to him most is the fast pace of attacks and the agent's initiative to accomplish the user's goals.

"At GitGuardian, we wanted to see how Artex handles secrets, so we ran it in a sealed lab," he says. "Artex ships no secret scanner, yet in every run where it acted, it found eight of the nine secrets. This included an AWS key recovered from git history. The model improvises on its hunt to reach the Artex user's goals."

Matt Snyder, Aviatrix head of security operations and threat research, says he was most surprised at how, despite the sophisticated nature of Artex's framework, the operational maturity of many threat actors deploying it appears to be low (given how many hosts remain Internet-exposed).

"AI is lowering the skill floor for offensive operations without improving operational discipline. The framework may be sophisticated, but the operational security surrounding many deployments is not," Snyder says. "This creates a dangerous combination in which more people can launch capable attacks, while poor security leaves their infrastructure, tooling, and potentially victim information exposed to anyone on the Internet."

Increasing sophistication for lower-grade attackers means, as always, defenders should be ready. Microsoft's Storm-3358 blog includes extensive indicators of compromise and recommends considering tools like defensive honeypots, which trick attackers into thinking they netted a valuable target.

Check Point advised in a blog post last week that organizations should expect greater automated pressure against exposed infrastructure. "Internet-facing systems should be continuously tested and hardened, with particular attention paid to weak authentication, exposed APIs, credential leakage, remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities and cloud storage permissions," the blog post read.

Censys principal security researcher Silas Cutler offered encouraging words. Because the underlying tradecraft is conventional, the fundamentals still hold, he said, "Enforce MFA, monitor your attack surface, and practice good credential hygiene."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

#10131. UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models

Parliamentary committee says tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety

UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far.

In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed.

It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation.

The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta.

All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything.

"We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP.

Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation.

"Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested."

The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers.

The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns.

MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny.

Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses.

There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology.

"AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne said. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear."

MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases.

Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®

#10130. Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics

Over the past month, Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon brought frontier physical reasoning to robotics: understanding 3D scenes, reconstructing real environments in simulation, practicing tasks in sim before running them on hardware, and directly controlling robot arms from camera images. Last week, we introduced Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning to a much faster model built for speed and efficiency.

To help developers put Hydrogen to work, today we're launching the Robotics plugin on Google Antigravity: a set of skills for hardware onboarding, simulation and robot control turning Antigravity into a one-stop robotics workbench. Together, they enable a developer to go from a robot in a box to one that can perform a working application in an afternoon. To install the plugin, open Antigravity, go to Customizations and search for Robotics on the Build With Google shelf.

Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon showed that a general model can drive a robot arm directly, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen preserves that ability. Give it a goal in plain language and a camera view, and it plans the task, writes and runs the control code, and keeps adjusting until the job is done. On the Artificial Analysis Robotics 0.1 benchmark, Gemini 4 Hydrogen controls a real 6-axis arm through eight everyday tabletop tasks, from pouring a drink to packing blocks into a box. Hydrogen scores 58, similar to Argon at a lower cost per token.

Hydrogen brings the specialized skills of our Gemini Robotics ER 2 (Embodied Reasoning) models into the core Gemini 4 model series, and it beats them on nearly every axis. On the public ERQA benchmark, Hydrogen outperforms Gemini Robotics ER 2 on spatial reasoning tasks such as multi-view correspondence and 3D trajectory reasoning. For developers using Gemini Robotics ER 2 today, we recommend trying out Gemini 4 Hydrogen for these workloads.

A fast, capable model is only half the story. Building a robot application has always meant gluing together drivers, calibration scripts, simulators, perception code, and a UI, which requires robotics expertise and a lot of time. The new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity packages that work into skills Gemini can use on your behalf:

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Here's what that looks like end to end: set up a robot and build real applications.

Starting from an empty desk, a developer plugs an I2RT YAM arm and an external depth camera into a laptop and asks Hydrogen in Antigravity to bring it up. The plugin's Skills install the software, find the camera, calibrate the arm, and run test motions. The arm is calibrated and ready for tasks in about 10 minutes. A similar flow also brings up a low-cost SO-ARM101 arm and an industrial grade FR3 Duo from scratch to live waving.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Once the robot is live, you can use a simple prompt to create a basic task within just a few minutes:

Once the robot is live, the next step is building a simulation you can trust. With the Robotics plugin, MuJoCo runs directly inside Antigravity with dedicated creation, auditing, and rendering skills. This allows you to build and preview high-quality simulated scenes and assets—whether described, imported from links/documents, or uploaded via workspace photos—right alongside your code. You can then "vibe sim" by adjusting shapes, positions, and physical properties through chat to verify reaching and grasping before deploying to physical hardware.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

The workbench with Hydrogen and Robotics plugins lets you go from an idea to a repeatable working application in real world in a much shorter time, by iterating and validating it in simulation.

A developer starts with a whiteboard sketch: a conveyor belt carrying mixed snacks, with a robot arm picking and sorting them into bins. From one prompt of the task with images of a real scene, Hydrogen constructs an interactive MuJoCo simulation of the cell, testing and validating the grasping policy in sim across multiple runs. The developer then deploys the verified policy directly to the robot in the real world. When nuances emerge (such as tuning gripper closure force or refining sorting rules), the developer iterates in natural language, asking Hydrogen to adjust the controller to iterate. Within about an hour end-to-end, the arm reliably sorts snacks off the moving belt.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Hydrogen's efficiency makes it practical to run a multi-step robot application all day. In this example, a developer uses Hydrogen to build a small web storefront for a soap shop, then connects it to two YAM Pro arms. When an order comes in, the arms set out a packing bin, pick the ordered mint and citrus bars, and pull a printed thank-you note from a printer.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

With just a few prompts, the FR3 Duo simulates a chess board and then can play chess against itself or take on human opponents.

Sorry, your browser doesn't support playback for this video

Gemini 4 Argon pushes the ceiling of physical reasoning. Gemini 4 Hydrogen makes those capabilities fast and affordable enough to use every day, and the Antigravity Robotics plugin puts them in a workbench where anyone can go from a robot in a box to a working application. We can't wait to see what you build.

You can share your own creations and use cases on the plugin’s GitHub discussions page. If you have any ideas, custom skills, or derived work you think would be helpful, please let us know—we’ll keep improving the plugins.

#10129. AWS Lambda now supports GPU instances for Event Functions on Lambda Managed Instances

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

GPU support is now available for EC2 G-series GPU instances for Event Functions running on AWS Lambda Managed Instances (LMI). You can now run GPU-accelerated workloads, including machine learning inference, media processing, rendering, and scientific computing, on GPU instances with serverless simplicity. GPU-accelerated functions are deployed as container (Open Container Initiative, OCI) images. You build an OCI image, point the function at it, and let Lambda handle provisioning, scaling, and event integration. There are no GPU drivers, CUDA versions, or AMIs to reconcile, and no clusters or device plugins to operate. GPU-accelerated functions run on the same Lambda Managed Instances foundation that already gives you Amazon EC2 pricing and specialized compute without managing servers.

Why customers need this Customers keep asking to run GPU workloads with the simplicity of serverless. Building on self-managed GPU infrastructure means selecting instances, installing and reconciling GPU drivers and CUDA libraries, planning capacity, writing scaling logic, and hand-building the event integrations that connect the GPU step to the rest of the application. Serverless GPU services that hide that work often sit outside your AWS environment, with no native event sources, identity, or networking.

Cost is the second problem. GPUs are expensive, and utilization is usually low because a single workload rarely saturates a GPU. A small inference task can leave most of a provisioned GPU idle while you pay for the whole thing.

This feature closes both gaps. You bring a function, and Lambda runs it on a GPU in minutes, triggered by the same AWS events as any other Lambda Event Function, billed and secured the same way. It also maximizes utilization of every GPU you pay for, by consolidating functions onto instances and keeping GPUs busy across concurrent requests.

What you can build You can run both AI/ML inference and non-ML workloads using GPU-accelerated compute on Lambda Managed Instances. This capability is optimized for inference rather than training, and custom models rather than large foundation models already available on services like Amazon Bedrock. Common workloads include:

Part of the Lambda programming model A GPU-accelerated function is one step in a larger application, and it composes with the rest of Lambda. Lambda durable functions orchestrate multi-step, long-running workflows around the GPU step, with checkpointing and automatic recovery. Lambda MicroVMs run untrusted or model-generated code in isolated, stateful sandboxes. In an agentic workload, a MicroVM executes the tool-use logic on CPU, then calls a GPU-accelerated function running on Lambda Managed Instances for inference.

GPU-accelerated functions also support the extended function timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, up to 90 minutes for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations, so you can run batch and other long-running GPU jobs, such as media transcoding or multi-step inference, without re-architecting. GPU-accelerated functions support container images up to 32 GB (10 GB per file), up to 32 GB of ephemeral storage, 2,048 to 32,768 MB of memory, 3 to 48 GB of accelerator memory, up to 48 concurrent requests per execution environment, and up to 15,000 vCPUs per capacity provider.

Let’s try it out To show what this looks like in practice, I deployed an open-source large language model (LLM) from Hugging Face as a Lambda function and sent it a prompt. With the vLLM base image from Lambda, I only set the Hugging Face model ID in the MODEL_ID environment variable, without writing any inference code. I used Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, a small instruction-tuned model that suits in-application tasks such as summarization, classification, and extraction. The flow has four steps: create a capacity provider, build and push the container image, create a function from that image, then publish and invoke. Before you begin, request an increase to your G-series instance quota (listed as Running On-Demand G and VT instances), because new accounts might start with a quota of 0. For more information, see On-Demand Instance quotas.

First, I created a capacity provider, where I specify the GPU instance types Lambda can use and let it auto-scale. Listing several instance types lets Lambda pick the most cost-effective one that is available and fall back across generations when capacity is tight.

The Lambda console shows the new capacity provider, lmi-gpu-cp, in the Active state. Note the VPC configuration with its subnets and security group.

Figure 1: The capacity provider is Active, with its VPC configuration.

Next, I built the container image. Lambda provides a curated vLLM base image that includes the vLLM inference server, PyTorch, Transformers, and the CUDA toolkit, along with a runtime interface client that supports concurrent invocations. The image serves the model for me, so I don’t write a handler or any inference server code. My entire Dockerfile is one line:

After pushing the image to Amazon ECR, I created the function. I chose the model with the MODEL_ID environment variable, which accepts a Hugging Face or ModelScope repository, an Amazon S3 location, or a local path. Lambda downloads the model, manages GPU memory, and serves requests. Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct is a public model, so I didn’t need a Hugging Face token. For private or gated models, or to get higher download rate limits, you can also set HF_TOKEN.

GPU-accelerated functions use AcceleratorConfig to request accelerator memory. AcceleratorMemorySize is the minimum GPU memory the function needs, and Lambda places the execution environment on the smallest available GPU that meets it, so the GPU you get can have more memory than you requested. I set PerExecutionEnvironmentMaxConcurrency to 4, the default. The vLLM server batches concurrent requests on the GPU, so invocations share one copy of the model and the GPU stays busy. I also set ExecutionEnvironmentMemoryGiBPerVCpu to 4, which gives the function the 16,384 MB of memory and 4 vCPUs it needs while leaving capacity on the 2xlarge instance for Lambda’s management components.

The function overview shows what makes this a GPU-accelerated function: the attached capacity provider that supplies the GPU instances and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR, all wired into the same function model you already use.

Figure 2: The lmi-gpu-inference function overview, showing the attached capacity provider and the vLLM container image deployed from Amazon ECR.

Functions on Lambda Managed Instances run from a published version, so I published one. Publishing provisions the execution environments, and each one downloads the model weights and warms up the engine before the version becomes active. The cold start happens during the publish step, so the first caller doesn’t wait for it.

Then I sent the model a prompt. The payload is a standard OpenAI request body: a messages array routes to chat completions, and a prompt field routes to text completions.

The model answered from a GPU inside the Lambda execution environment, and the response is a standard OpenAI completion object, so any OpenAI-compatible client works with it.

Four concurrent invocations finished in about the same time as a single one, on one execution environment that shares one copy of the model in GPU memory. From a Hugging Face model ID to a live, OpenAI-compatible GPU endpoint took about 10 minutes, most of it unattended while Lambda provisioned capacity and warmed up the model.

That’s a working LLM endpoint with no inference server code, no GPU drivers, and no cluster to manage. To try a different model, I update MODEL_ID and publish a new version, with no image rebuild. Each version is an immutable snapshot, so different models can run side by side as separate versions. It is also a Lambda Event Function, so I can trigger it from an Amazon SQS queue to process documents in batches, put Amazon API Gateway in front of it, or call it as the inference step in a Lambda durable functions workflow.

For production, copy the model weights to an S3 bucket in the same Region, point MODEL_ID at that bucket, and set VLLM_LOAD_FORMAT=runai_streamer so the weights stream straight into memory. This gives faster starts and removes the dependency on the Hugging Face Hub. For more guidance, see the best practices for running inference workloads. Beyond LLM inference, you can also run custom ML inference, media processing, and other GPU workloads. See the Lambda documentation for best practices.

The configuration tab shows the settings that matter for a GPU-accelerated function: 16,384 MB of memory, the 15-minute timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage for the downloaded weights, alongside the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency of 4, the 4:1 memory-to-vCPU ratio, and 16 GB of accelerator memory.

Figure 3: The function’s configuration, including memory, timeout, and 32 GB of ephemeral storage, and the function-level capacity provider settings: per-environment concurrency, the memory-to-vCPU ratio, and accelerator memory.

When you finish testing, delete the function and then the capacity provider so that Lambda stops the GPU instances and you stop paying for them.

How it works The capabilities below are what you get out of the box, each one removing GPU work you would otherwise own.

Skip the GPU software setup. Curated base images ship with the frameworks and tools handled for you, so you do not install or reconcile them: base:cuda (CUDA toolkit and runtime), cupy:cuda (CuPy, NumPy, SciPy, Pandas, Numba), pytorch:cuda (PyTorch, torchvision, torchaudio, transformers, FFmpeg), and serving images vllm:cuda and sglang:cuda. Use them directly, extend them, or bring a fully custom image.

No GPU infrastructure to operate. Lambda handles driver compatibility, provisioning, routing, and load balancing, so you ship functions instead of running GPU fleets. Deploy with the same Console, CLI, AWS CloudFormation, AWS CDK, AWS SAM, and Terraform workflow as any Lambda Event Function.

Trigger GPU work from any AWS event. The same 200+ event sources that trigger Event Functions, including Amazon S3, Amazon SQS, Amazon API Gateway, and Amazon EventBridge, trigger GPU-accelerated functions directly, with the same scaling, error handling, and retries. No custom integration code.

Serve concurrent requests on each GPU. Each execution environment can process multiple concurrent invocations on the same GPU, which you control with the per-environment concurrency setting. Raising it packs more requests onto each GPU instance to drive utilization up, so you get more throughput from the capacity you already pay for.

Multiple instance types. Specify multiple instance types or generations, and Lambda selects the most cost-effective available option and falls back across your list to reduce Insufficient Capacity Errors.

Capacity options. GPU instances run as Amazon EC2 On-Demand instances, and your existing Savings Plans and Reserved Instances apply. For predictable GPU availability, create an EC2 On-Demand Capacity Reservation (ODCR) that matches your capacity provider configuration, and Lambda uses that reserved capacity automatically.

Large container images and storage. Container images up to 32 GB are supported, along with up to 32 GB of NVMe ephemeral storage in /tmp. Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading lets your function begin executing before the full image is downloaded, which reduces execution environment startup time by up to 70%.

See GPU usage without extra setup. GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization appear alongside standard function metrics in Amazon CloudWatch and in the AWS Lambda console.

After invoking the function, the console surfaces the GPU-specific metrics next to the standard ones. Track GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization to see how much of the accelerator each invocation actually uses, which is the signal that drives both auto-scaling and cost.

Figure 4: GPU utilization, GPU memory utilization, GPU memory used, and GPU power utilization for the vLLM function under concurrent load.

Pricing and availability This feature is generally available today, supporting the Amazon EC2 G-series (G4dn, G5, G6, G6f, Gr6, Gr6f, G6e) at launch, with more instance families to come. You pay the underlying EC2 instance fee (eligible for Savings Plans and Reserved Instances), plus a 9.75 percent management fee for GPU instances, and the standard Lambda request fee of $0.20 per million requests. For pricing and Region availability, see AWS Lambda pricing.

You can also build with your AI coding assistants and agents: explore the Builder Center and connect your tools with the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which bundles the AWS MCP Server and curated agent skills.

To get started, visit the AWS Lambda console and see the GPU-accelerated functions documentation.

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. A three-time Ironman finisher and four-time re:Invent speaker, he brings the same endurance mindset to building cloud solutions.

#10128. Newer Models, Same Advantage

Three months ago, we published a paper on DharmaOCR and open-sourced one of the models. The objective was specific: optical character recognition engineered for Brazilian Portuguese.

The training pipeline was built in two stages. The first was a supervised fine-tuning step, drawing on a broad collection of Portuguese-language files from different sources, formats, and levels of complexity. This stage aligned the model's weights to the specific vocabulary, syntax, and document structures of Brazilian Portuguese — concentrating representational capacity on the target language rather than distributing it across a broader multilingual space. The second stage applied Direct Preference Optimization: rather than training only on correct transcriptions, the model learned from comparative preference data between competing outputs, teaching it to consistently select the better extraction at inference time. This stage addressed a different problem: not accuracy, but stability. By suppressing the failure modes that cause generative models to produce repetitive or incoherent output, DPO reduced inference time and cost, and materially improved the reliability of what the model delivered in production.

The combined result was a model that achieved the highest extraction quality score with the lowest degeneration rate on a Portuguese-focused benchmark. Both stages were necessary. The fine-tuning stage built domain competency; the DPO stage ensured that competency held under the conditions where models tend to fail.

OCR models have been moving quickly. But the gaps that originally motivated DharmaOCR's design (in extraction quality on complex documents and in model stability under production conditions) have not closed. They have, if anything, become more instructive as the field has changed.

The proliferation of multimodal generative models made language model-based OCR widely accessible, and the wave of fine-tuned OCR variants that followed reflects how fast that adoption has moved. That proliferation has not, however, changed the fundamental character of the technology. Every OCR system built on a generative model is probabilistic. Transcription errors are an inherent variable of this probabilistic technology. What differentiates models is how many errors they make and of what kind. That is determined by two things: the structure of the model (its architecture and parameter count) and how those parameters were trained for the task.

Architecture and parameter count establish the ceiling on what a model can learn. Training determines how that capacity is allocated.

This distinction is where specialization becomes a structural question rather than a design preference. When a model is trained on a restricted domain — a single language, a bounded document type, a specific task — All of its parameters are dedicated to that specific task. When a model is trained to cover a broader range of domains — a multilingual model handling N languages, for instance — those same parameters must be distributed across all of them. The distribution is not linear: the neuron superposition principle means individual parameters can encode multiple features simultaneously. But the division is real, and its consequences are real. A model covering more ground commits less to any given part of it.

DharmaOCR was trained to accept that constraint in reverse. The model is not designed to be the best option for other languages, and was never intended to be. In exchange, every parameter available to the network could be oriented toward the specific vocabulary, morphology, and orthographic patterns of Brazilian Portuguese — the most directed possible use of the model's resources for that domain.

That concentration is the structural basis of an inherent advantage over multilingual and broader-domain models. The advantage does not depend on having a larger architecture or a more sophisticated training procedure than competitors use — new architectures and new training techniques improve what any model can do. It depends on where those resources are directed: at one domain rather than spread across many.

Three months later, newer models have arrived. Whether the case for specialization holds when those models are newer and more capable is a different question.

Three months after the DharmaOCR paper appeared, two new OCR models attracted significant attention from the research community: Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR. Both represent genuine technical advances — new training techniques, new datasets, and strong results across multiple languages on a range of benchmark evaluations. They are the kind of models that raise the competitive standard for what OCR systems are expected to deliver.

When we ran both against the DharmaOCR benchmark — an evaluation designed exclusively around Portuguese — the results were conclusive.

DharmaOCR scored 0.925. Mistral OCR4 scored 0.798. Unlimited-OCR scored 0.7587.

The difference is significant. Mistral OCR4 falls approximately 13 points below DharmaOCR; Unlimited-OCR falls more than 16 points below. Both were released after our model, both backed by substantial research resources. On a task where DharmaOCR's fundamental design decision was to concentrate entirely on Portuguese, the specialization advantage is measurable and significant.

The benchmark is the central finding. What follows illustrates why the gap takes the specific shape it does.

Processing non-trivial Portuguese documents reveals precisely where multilingual models tend to break. ENEM essays (Brazil's national high school examination) combine handwritten text with vocabulary, proper nouns, and cultural references that are specific to Brazilian Portuguese. They are exactly the kind of documents where language-specific training produces a return.

Figure 1: ENEM essay manuscript used in benchmark evaluation with outputs of the each model. Misreads marked in red.

Mistral OCR4, evaluated on documents of this kind, transcribed the name Chico Buarque (one of Brazil's most widely recognized musicians and poets) as "Chico Barque." Unlimited-OCR rendered the same name as "chico bique." Confronted with the phrase "O Brasil não exclui, assimila" ("Brazil does not exclude, it assimilates", a Chico Buarque quotation embedded in the same document) Unlimited-OCR returned: "a dose de chico bique, 'o Brasil no exclu, eliminila.'

These are not random errors. A model with insufficient exposure to Brazilian Portuguese does not fail arbitrarily — it fails at precisely the vocabulary and proper nouns that distinguish Brazilian Portuguese from the broader multilingual corpus. Chico Buarque is not an obscure reference; the name is nationally recognized. Its systematic corruption across outputs is not an edge case. It is a diagnostic: evidence of where the model's training did not go.

DharmaOCR, evaluated on the same documents, handles these cases correctly. The reason is direct: the model's training was concentrated on this linguistic space, orienting its resources toward the vocabulary and proper noun distributions that characterize Brazilian Portuguese rather than spreading them across many languages at once.

The examples illustrate the benchmark rather than replace it. The benchmark establishes the magnitude of the gap; the examples show why it is concentrated in language-specific recognition rather than in general capability.

Extraction accuracy, however, is only one dimension of production performance. Stability under visual difficulty is another — and operationally, it is the more consequential one to fail on.

When a generative model encounters a document it cannot clearly resolve — small fonts, degraded scan quality, dense handwriting — it faces uncertainty in its input signal. Models trained primarily on next-token prediction objectives face a specific vulnerability here: when the visual signal becomes ambiguous, the model can continue generating from prior learned patterns rather than from the source document. The result is text degeneration — output that is repetitive, incoherent, and semantically disconnected from the page.

Presented with a document with small fonts, Mistral OCR4 produces output with no connection to what is written.

Figure 3: DharmaOCR output and Mistral OCR4 degenerated output

This is not a low-quality transcription of the source. It is a failure of an entirely different category.

The operational consequence is distinct from that of a transcription error. An incorrect transcription is wrong in a recoverable way — it stands in a relationship to the source document, and the error can in principle be identified and corrected. Degenerated output has no such relationship. It cannot be corrected because there is nothing to correct toward. For downstream processes that depend on structured OCR output — document classification, information extraction, compliance workflows — degenerated output is not inaccurate data. It is structurally unusable data. The efficiency that automation was meant to deliver is negated at precisely the point where output stops being information.

Mistral OCR4 and Unlimited-OCR are good models with significant technical advances behind them. The degeneration behavior described here does not define them; it identifies a specific failure condition that their current training has not addressed for this domain. The question is what a training pipeline designed to address it looks like.

In DharmaOCR, the answer is the DPO stage.

Supervised fine-tuning concentrates the model's resources on the target domain — the stage that builds the linguistic alignment described above. But SFT trains on individual token predictions: the model learns to produce the correct next token given the context preceding it. Under visual complexity, this creates the condition that produces degeneration. If an early token in the output diverges from the source document, each subsequent prediction is conditioned on that divergent state, and the output continues to drift. Repetition loops and incoherent sequences are an inherent characteristic in this context — they are the predictable result of an objective optimized step by step without accounting for the coherence of the full extraction.

DPO trains against a different signal. Where SFT trains token by token, DPO trains the model against the quality of complete outputs — teaching it to discriminate between competing responses based on the coherence of the full extraction rather than the accuracy of individual predictions. The effect is stabilizing: on documents where visual complexity would otherwise trigger drift, the model is less likely to commit to a divergent path, because its training penalized outputs that lost coherence at the extraction level.

The result is what the original benchmark demonstrated: lower degeneration rates alongside higher extraction accuracy, on the same documents where models without this training stage lose coherence.

The benchmark establishes what is true today. It is less precise about what will be true in two years.

It is possible — and likely — that newer models will eventually outperform the current DharmaOCR even in Brazilian Portuguese. Architectures will improve. Training techniques will advance. Datasets will expand. The field moves toward higher capability at every level, and there is no reason to expect that trajectory to stop. This is expected, and it is welcome.

What changes with each architectural generation is the ceiling on absolute performance. What does not change is the structural logic that determines which systems come closest to their ceiling in a given domain.

Available resources — compute, parameters, training data — are finite. They must be directed somewhere. A system that directs them at a single domain will extract more from them in that domain than a system distributing the same resources across many. This relationship holds regardless of how capable the generalist model has become. The gap between specialist and generalist may evolve as architectures improve. The structural dynamic does not reverse. We explored this principle in more depth in an earlier piece on why specialization continues to produce an advantage as AI systems advance (Why Specialization Is Inevitable).

This is what shapes how Dharma approaches what comes next. The objective is not to defend the current model's benchmark position. It is to remain at the frontier of emerging techniques — new architectures, new training methods, new approaches to alignment and evaluation — and adapt them toward the same end: a specialized system for Brazilian Portuguese OCR that makes the best possible use of available resources, at the lowest possible cost and the shortest possible inference time.

Better tools do not work against specialization. They expand what it can achieve.

Three months ago, we showed that concentrating a model's training on a specific domain produces a measurable advantage over generalist systems, including ones that are newer and better-resourced. That advantage held. The same principle will determine how DharmaOCR continues to evolve — not by staying fixed, but by applying whatever progress the field makes to a domain that remains fixed.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

#10127. November Patch Tuesday: An Overflowing Cornucopia of CVEs

Microsoft serves up an actively exploited Outlook zero-day, and a wave of critical Exchange, SharePoint, Windows Search, and LDAP bugs that exhausted defenders need to prioritize fast.

November offers up a veritable Patch Tuesday feast of vulnerabilities that are more likely to be exploited. In its second four-digit Patch Tuesday release in a row, Microsoft today addressed 1,093 security vulnerabilities, with 63 rated critical, and one zero-day in the mix (CVE-2026-124194, CVSS 6.5) that Microsoft confirmed is under active exploit.

"Most security teams haven't quite recovered from the last month of bumper-to-bumper critical vulnerabilities, emergency patches, and '2shell'-branded everything, and we're yet again at another Patch Tuesday," says Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at Watchtowr.

"Teams are really starting to feel the strain of working out what actually matters when there is fire after fire every day demanding immediate attention," he adds. "Our advice hasn't changed … start with what you actually have exposed to the Internet, then what's already being exploited in the wild, and only then everything else. Before going into panic mode, check whether you even use the vulnerable component, or meet the prerequisites for exploitation."

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

To that end, security teams should prioritize CVE-2026-124194, and not just because attackers are already targeting it. It's a spoofing vulnerability in Outlook that may not allow code execution, hence its moderate severity rating, but could allow the disclosure of an account’s NTLMv2 hash — and in turn, the target's login.

"To exploit it, an attacker sends a target a malicious Office file and convinces them to open it," explained Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable, in his monthly Patch Tuesday commentary. "If the attack succeeds, the attacker captures the victim's NT LAN Manager v2 (NTLMv2) hash, a value derived from their Windows password. The attacker may be able to relay it to other systems to sign in as the user, or crack it to recover the password."

Security teams should also prioritize a pair of critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, in Exchange and SharePoint, respectively, that each open targets to any attacker with a low-privilege login.

The first, in Exchange Server (CVE-2026-118207, CVSS 8.8), "belongs in this week's emergency window for every Exchange Server Subscription Edition server you run," Automox researchers warned in their monthly Patch Tuesday bulletin, and "all an attacker needs to start is a low-level login."

It's an improper input validation that could allow an authenticated attacker with low-level access to send the server a specially crafted request and run code with no user interaction.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

"Code on an Exchange server reaches every mailbox it hosts," warned Automox researchers. "And Exchange usually holds broad rights in Active Directory, so the mailboxes are just the start."

Meanwhile, an important-rated flaw (CVE-2026-120002, CVSS 9.9) in SharePoint Server is an elevation of privilege vulnerability that needs quick addressing, according to Automox.

"The flaw is incorrect authorization," the researchers noted. "That 9.9 comes from a changed scope: a successful attack reaches past the vulnerable SharePoint component itself. An attacker who already holds a low-privileged account sends requests over the network and elevates their privileges, with no user interaction required."

Another critical RCE to watch out for, according to Automox, is CVE-2026-110043 (CVSS 8.8/10), a one-click heap-based buffer overflow in Outlook that uses the Preview Pane as an attack vector. A target must select a weaponized email so it displays in the Preview Pane for it to trigger the attacker's code, which runs with that user's permissions.

"Patch internet-facing Exchange and SharePoint servers, and book the Exchange restart now," the Automox researchers advised. "Push the Office update this week, then check the installed build, because a fully patched Windows dashboard says nothing about Office. Rank by score and assessment, not label."

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at the Zero Day Initiative (ZDI), also identified a Windows Search RCE (CVE-2026-116928, CVSS 9.8) as needing immediate attention.

"We start with Windows Search, which is reached through Exchange Server," he said in his November Patch Tuesday blog post, where he also listed 30 potentially wormable CVEs to patch quickly. "This bug allows an unauthenticated attacker to send an email with a specially crafted attachment that triggers the bug when the server automatically indexes it. The recipient never opens anything. It is a zero-click code execution bug on a high-value target. It’s also a CVSS 9.8 and clearly more severe than any of the nine patches Exchange receives this month."

And finally, Childs pointed to CVE-2026-119958, an RCE bug in Windows Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP).

"This patch addresses a bug that allows an unauthenticated attacker to exploit an out-of-bounds (OOB) write (CWE-787) by sending crafted LDAP calls over the network, with no user interaction," he warned. "Since it runs code in the LDAP service context, it could be quite destructive, especially on Domain Controllers. Test and deploy this one quickly."

Childs also recommended testing and deploying patches for the wormable bugs quickly, especially for network-facing services like DNS, DHCP, LDAP, and Exchange.

While the cornucopia of CVEs this month, especially on the heels of the record October Patch Tuesday, may feel overwhelming, security teams should stick to best practices and not get overwhelmed, advises Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra.

"I don't know about everyone else, but I'm tired," he says via email, adding that he believes that, eventually, AI will finish turning up old bugs and teams can once again look forward to smaller Patch Tuesday releases. "I can only imagine that if I’m tired, admins and operations teams everywhere are also tired. I believe that we will make it through to the other side, if we prioritize updates and focus on what really matters. The noise is coming at us from all sides, and we need to cut through it and figure out what really matters to the business."

Tara Seals is an award-winning journalist with 25+ years of experience as a reporter, analyst, and editor in the cybersecurity, communications, and technology spaces. As managing editor, she runs the newsroom at Dark Reading, leading a team of staff writers and freelance contributors. She also heads up strategy for a variety of in-depth, multichannel news coverage initiatives.

Prior to joining Dark Reading in 2022, Tara was editor-in-chief at cybersecurity stalwart Threatpost, and prior to that, the North American news lead for Infosecurity Magazine. She also spent 13 years working for other titles at Virgo Publishing (now part of Informa TechTarget), as executive editor and editor-in-chief at publications focused on communications service providers, channel partners, and enterprise mobile and video technology. In 2026, she was awarded a regional Azbee award for her in-depth coverage of the ongoing North Korean fake worker cyber campaign.
