Git is releasing updates addressing six security vulnerabilities affecting clones, reference handling, merges, binary patches, and imports. Here is what users need to know.

Editor’s note (November 17, 2026): This post has been updated with additional CVE information and updated guidance for GitHub Enterprise Server users. Please see the release information below for the versions that include the fixes.

Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.An attacker-controlled Git server can exploit this discrepancy to replace a clone’s .git file or directory, redirecting Git to attacker-controlled configuration or hooks.For recursive clones, this can execute attacker-controlled code during the clone. For non-recursive clones, an attacker can replace the top-level .git directory with a file pointing to attacker-controlled repository metadata. The clone can then report an error and recommend running git status in the resulting directory; following that advice can execute attacker-controlled code.The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Robert Chen reported CVE-2026-111760, which was fixed by Elijah Newren and Toon Claes, with help from Johannes Schindelin and Jeff King. Luke Martin reported CVE-2026-113408, which was fixed by Toon Claes.

pwn2addr reported CVE-2026-114466, CVE-2026-114467, and CVE-2026-114469, which were fixed by Karthik Nayak. Kaartic Sivaraam implemented the fix for CVE-2026-105437 based on a patch by Jeff King, with help from Toon Claes and Christian Couder.

Elijah Newren is a Staff Software Engineer at GitHub. He is the designer and implementer of merge-ort, Git's default merge strategy since 2.34, author of git-filter-repo—the history rewriting tool the Git project officially recommends—and a driving force behind sparse-checkout.

#10106. AI Raises the Stakes for Cyber Resilience

An organization's ability to quickly recover from a business disruption will be a competitive advantage in an era of AI-driven threats and business enablement.

Commvault SHIFT — Nashville, Tenn. — Enterprise data recovery practices must evolve from a last-resort response to a continuous operational discipline focused on minimizing business disruption and containing the blast radius of cyber incidents as quickly as possible.

That was the central message at Commvault's SHIFT 2026 conference this week, where security executives highlighted the growing importance of making operational resilience a business priority as AI-driven threats and increasingly autonomous business processes complicate the task of maintaining continuity.

"AI is changing the durable advantage you have built for your business, your brand, your supply chain, your data," said Sanjay Mirchandani, president and CEO of Commvault, in a keynote address at the event. "In the AI era, resilience will be your new competitive advantage."

Two developments are driving the trend. On the threat side, AI is giving attackers the ability to automate and accelerate reconnaissance, exploit development, social engineering, and lateral movement. The trend has compressed the time organizations have to detect and contain an intrusion, Mirchandani and other executives at the event noted.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

At the same time, enterprises are increasingly embedding AI into business processes, workflows and decision-making, creating new dependencies on data, applications and autonomous systems.

The result is a more complex operating environment in which a disruption can have wider and faster consequences, making the ability to contain incidents, preserve trusted operations and recover without derailing business activity more important than ever.

Attackers these days are able to move faster with a level of automation not available before, noted Rajeev Kottomtharayil, chief products officer at Commvault. Increasingly, recovery is becoming not just about speed but bringing back clean data. "If everything is under attack, how do we know what to trust? The real goal is to have a clean, safe space to recover even if everything around you has been compromised," Kottomtharayil said.

Business innovation and enablement are also driving the need for greater operational resilience. Resilient operations give organizations the confidence to experiment with AI and put it to work across the business, while ensuring they can recover quickly when something goes wrong, said Pragnesh Dave, head of generative AI and ML sales at AWS. "AI is collapsing the amount of time it takes to move from an idea to an outcome," he said during a keynote session. As a result, the competitive advantage will come not simply from how quickly organizations can turn intelligence into action, but from how quickly they can do so while managing the risks and consequences when those actions sometimes prove wrong.

Related:Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

Dave pointed to the operations model at Amazon that emphasizes the notion of the "door swinging both ways" when teams try to innovate. It is an approach that has enabled teams at Amazon to code more than four times faster than before, he said.

"The question for everyone is not if something is going to break," he said. Rather, it is about what the blast radius is and the time it takes from when something breaks to recovering to the prior trusted state. "If something goes wrong, you need to be able to recover quickly. You should be able to walk back a decision. Think of your recovery time as your innovation project."

Continuous detection and continuous recovery are going to become a baseline requirement for organizations, argued Peter Diamandis, futurist, entrepreneur, and founder and chairman of the XPRIZE Foundation. Over the next few years, he foresees all organizations harnessing AI to migrate a significant workload to the "digital edge" with humans providing judgement, taste, and oversight. "AI gives us all access to capabilities that were once scarce." The qualities that matter the most will be the speed at which an organization can innovate and that requires standing up capabilities to recover quickly when failures do occur, he said during a keynote address.

Related:NIST Finalizes Post-Quantum Cryptography Guidance, GAO Offers a Reality Check

At the same time, recovery is not becoming a substitute for prevention, says Bill O'Connell, chief security officer at Commvault. Both are equally important. But "building the highest walls and the deepest moat" to keep threats out alone is no longer enough. Organizations have to equally focus on building an ability to recover quickly to a trusted state regardless of the reason for a disruption and to thoroughly test that ability before it becomes necessary.

The key to keep in mind is that while AI has dramatically accelerated the pace of change it hasn’t altered the need for traditional, and long-familiar, IT governance and controls around their assets, identities, access, authentication and authentication, O'Connell says. "The IT maintenance and housekeeping elements still matter." When organizations have supercharged tools which they are not entirely sure how to govern, they need to make sure those fundamentals remain in place.

In enabling better resilience, organizations should also evaluate what impact third parties could have on their ability to quickly restore operations, O'Connell says. For years, organizations have used questionnaires and external vendor risk-scoring services to try and assess third-party risk. In the AI era, security teams need to go a step further with their most critical suppliers, he adds. O'Connell suggested organizations have their technical architects work with their counterparts at third-party suppliers to understand how critical services are actually configured and what would happen if a provider experienced a breach or a disruption.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#10105. StubHub International warns customer data may have left the venue

Names and contact details potentially exposed, ticket reseller finds no evidence passwords or payment information were accessed

Ticket resale giant StubHub International has warned customers that a recent breach may have exposed their personal information to cybercriminals.

The company said it detected "unauthorized access to certain systems" on its platform between late October and early November.

Customer notification emails seen by The Register list potentially affected information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, and country or regional settings.

StubHub International, operated by Ticketbis S.L., apologized for the intrusion and offered the usual promise to implement security enhancements after the fact.

The company said it had addressed "certain vulnerabilities" while containing the incident and was continuing to monitor for suspicious activity.

Outside cybersecurity experts are assisting with the ongoing investigation. The company warned that any exposed information could be used to make subsequent scams more convincing.

"To date, we have found no evidence of unauthorised access to account passwords, banking information or payment card details," the email stated. "We also have no evidence that the compromised information has been used fraudulently.

"However, there is a risk that third parties could use this information to attempt fraud, identity theft or phishing through emails, messages or calls that appear to come from StubHub International or other trusted organizations."

The Register contacted StubHub International for more information, such as how many customers were affected, but it did not respond.

Digital Fuel Capital bought StubHub International from Viagogo in 2021 after the UK's Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) required the international business to be sold to address competition concerns.

In June, the CMA fined Ticketbis £889,200 and ordered refunds exceeding £590,000 after finding that mandatory fees were omitted from upfront ticket prices.

StubHub International also recently faced criticism for allowing a single ticket tout to advertise £1 million worth of U2 tickets, despite its stated opposition to ticket-buying bots. ®

Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

How many times this week did you re-explain the same task to an agent? How many times did you ask your colleague with deep institutional knowledge how to solve a specific problem? That context shouldn’t be lost in a chat or locked in one person’s head. Agent skills let you capture repeatable instructions so you and your agents can reuse them. The skill you write for yourself tonight can later become part of a team’s pipeline.

An agent skill is a versioned directory centered on a SKILL.md file that describes when and how to do a repeatable task. You can share those instructions across agents, but the environment still needs to provide the tools, credentials, and permissions to carry them out. A skill can describe how to query a database, for example, but it doesn’t grant access to that database.

I covered this topic live with Shishir Tewari, Senior Manager, Data Engineering at Procore, during GitHub Universe 2026. Our session was titled “Build once, run on any agent: a practical guide to agent skills”.

A skill works best when it has a clear job, input, and output. For example, let’s say you’re building an agent that checks AI-generated changes against the original request. If the same agent assesses its own work, its explanation might influence the review. With Proof Agent, we use a separate verifier to examine the changes and provide evidence for its findings. The skill’s frontmatter names the task and describes its purpose:

At the center is a simple rule: self-verification is not verification.

The When to Verify section in Proof Agent’s SKILL.md says when to invoke the skill. The remaining instructions explain what the verifier reviews and what evidence to include in its findings.

When the judgment that makes a data pipeline correct lives in four different people’s heads, those four people are the roadmap. Each change to the pipeline depends on their availability and knowledge of the data. Data Forge is an example of how to capture parts of that judgment in skills that work together.

In the support-desk pipeline example, we start with a request for metrics that count incidents created and resolved. Before building the pipeline, the forge-init skill discovers details such as source tables and naming conventions, then writes them to a resolved manifest. The other skills read that manifest for the project context they need.

The forge-builder skill then coordinates the work from the issue through to a pull request. It uses forge-dbx to query the data platform and forge-lint to apply the team’s standards as it designs and builds the pipeline. A person reviews the proposed decisions along the way, and the resulting pull request contains the pipeline code, schema changes, and tests.

Each skill has a defined responsibility, and they share project context instead of rediscovering it independently. When a step changes, you can change one skill and leave the rest alone.

Skills fit bounded, repeatable work that benefits from reusable judgment, such as a checklist, release, migration, or metric pipeline. If a workflow needs a stable interface, shared state, an audit trail, long-running control, or permissions enforced outside the model, an application is a better fit.

We don’t want to hardcode every project’s names, database, or conventions into the skills. In the Data Forge support-desk example, a manifest describes the project, metric store, and platform so the skills can use the right project details without baking them into their instructions:

With the discovered details in the resolved manifest, the other skills don’t have to make their own assumptions about the project.

Keep discovered project details separate from team standards. The forge-init initialization skill can inspect existing schemas and code patterns; the forge-lint skill supplies the rules to follow before code is generated. A pattern found in a repository isn’t automatically a rule to preserve, so make discovered details reviewable and let people confirm or change them where business judgment is needed. To check portability, ask: could another team use these skills with its own manifest without rewriting them?

The forge-dbx skill gives the other Data Forge skills one way to access the data platform. It reads the manifest and selects a Databricks or DuckDB adapter, so each skill doesn’t need its own connection and query logic.

The manifest can choose DuckDB for the local support-desk demo, but it can’t install the DuckDB CLI or grant database access. Those remain setup responsibilities for the environment and its user. The manifest picks the engine; the host provides the access.

The Data Forge support-desk workflow has seven phases, with a human checkpoint at each one. The workflow overview shows how the skills fit together. Before a phase proceeds, the workflow checks that the previous phase is complete; before schema changes run, it asks for approval.

The Proof Agent example applies the same principle to code review. A GitHub Actions workflow gives the verifier the original request and code changes, but not the coding agent’s own assessment. The verifier returns PASS, FAIL, or PARTIAL and must cite evidence in the changed files. The GitHub Action does a static review of the diff; it doesn’t execute code or run tests. In the demo workflow, we set block-on-fail: false so findings were advisory. By default, a FAIL fails the check, which blocks the merge if the check is required. The aim is to keep test results and merge requirements in your repository’s CI checks and rules.

Supporting multiple clients can mean keeping several copies of the same instructions in sync. In the Data Forge example, we keep skills/*/SKILL.md as the source and use a packaging script to generate client-specific files: .claude-plugin/plugin.json for Claude Code, .cursor-plugin/plugin.json for Cursor, and .github/agents/*.agent.md for GitHub Copilot. The script also includes a check mode for CI:

Clients can differ in their available models, tools, credentials, and permissions. After installing a skill, check that the client recognizes it for the intended task, loads its references, can use the required tools, and returns the evidence the skill calls for.

Start with the task you’re tired of explaining. Write down what it needs, where it stops, and what a reviewer sees. Then try it with another agent and improve it as you learn what works.

#10103. Meta is back with Muse Glimmer: local, agentic, multimodal, and open source

To celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:

In addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Muse Glimmer comes with day-0 support in transformers, both for the main model and the speculative decoding drafter. You can use AutoModelForMultimodalLM and AutoProcessor classes to load the model and the processor.

We also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model shows strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! We are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a New Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏

#10102. Space robot legend Voyager 1 is now more than 1 light-day away

As the world is hit by IT snafu after IT snafu, Voyager sails on, almost half a century after launch

NASA's Voyager 1 probe is now more than one light-day from Earth – so distant that a radio signal takes 24 hours to reach it. The veteran spacecraft has spent almost 50 years getting there.

Voyager 1 was launched on September 5, 1977, from Cape Canaveral in Florida. Planning for the mission began in the 1960s, while NASA was working feverishly to put a man on the Moon ahead of the Soviet Union.

A rare alignment of the outer planets made a tour of Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune possible. Voyager 2 eventually visited all four; Voyager 1's route prioritized Saturn's moon Titan, ruling out a subsequent encounter with Pluto.

Voyager 1 completed a flyby of Jupiter in 1979, and passed Saturn and Titan in 1980. Its final imaging sequence in 1990 produced the solar system "Family Portrait," including the famous Pale Blue Dot image of Earth. The cameras were then switched off for good.

Thirty-six years after those final pictures, Voyager 1 remains in contact with Earth, with two science instruments still operating: the magnetometer and plasma wave subsystem. Others have been shut down over the decades to conserve the dwindling power supplied by its radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs).

Dr Garry Hunt, a member of Voyager's original imaging team, told The Register: "Voyager's real success is the way it used reliable equipment. Well-tested Mariner equipment, and special new things that had come about for it.

"We had fault protection on board as well. If anything goes wrong, it automatically switches to a backup. So there was always a backup. There was always a safe mode. We had to have radiation protection on board … when we designed this, we didn't really know the magnetic environment around Jupiter, and to be told it was so strong, 1,000 times stronger than we anticipated, really threw everything up in the air, and so that had to be dealt with."

Hunt paid tribute to the succession of project managers and engineers who have kept the probe running over the years. "I think this was a really wonderful example of project management, of clever management of engineering, and interesting science coming out of it, which has made history books and gone to be a catalyst for other things in the future," he said.

Voyager 1 may now take two days to answer a call from Earth. After almost 50 years, the remarkable thing is that it still answers at all. ®

#10101. Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

Knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

The distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

The standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

Dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:

The GIF below shows the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

The table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only shows up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

The efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

The student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss

In October, we experienced eight incidents that resulted in degraded performance across GitHub services.

We continue to share monthly updates on the work behind GitHub’s availability and reliability.

The short version of October: we added substantial independently scalable Azure capacity and removed several ways that failures could escalate. However, write outages, monitoring gaps during data migrations, and a regional network disruption reinforced the need for capacity growth to be paired with safer operations, stronger isolation, and validated regional recovery.

As of November 9, 140 of 151 production services and 32 of 50 MySQL primaries were running in Azure Central US. Azure served 63% of migrated-service reads, 66% of monolith reads, and 52% of Git reads. We also completed a compute expansion across all nine Central US Kubernetes clusters, more than doubling capacity.

That capacity is already carrying real growth. Migrated-service traffic has increased 82% since March, with Central US absorbing the growth beyond the highest weekly-average load previously served from our existing datacenter. This gives GitHub more room to grow without pushing the original environment beyond its prior operating range.

We also made several targeted reliability improvements. Actions changes increased capacity for critical Azure control-plane requests. A separate NAT-gateway mitigation reduced usage by 85%; four production jobs failed during the change, compared with approximately 800 expected without the mitigation. Connection limits and other client improvements now also reduce the chance that a dependency interruption becomes a broader reconnect storm.

We removed concentrated sources of database load as well. A high-traffic GitHub Actions endpoint handling more than 250 million requests per day moved to a more efficient service path, reducing peak database reads by 85%. Requiring at least three characters before searching repository topics reduced slow or terminated queries for that pattern by approximately 98%.

Reliability was still not where it needed to be. The October 7 write outages exposed an unsafe interaction between database orchestration and production routing. An October 29 Azure network disruption affected all three Central US availability zones and at least 34,128 signed-in users. More details on these and other incidents follow.

The East US 3 buildout is about one week behind plan. The next phase starts with its first validated traffic ramp in the first week of December, while we continue hardening migration safety, dependency isolation, and regional recovery.

The principle remains the same: availability, then capacity, then features.

Duration: approximately 3 hours and 45 minutes.

Customers may have seen GitHub Actions jobs on GitHub-hosted runners stay queued much longer than usual, and some workflow runs failed to start. During the worst stretch, which lasted about 90 minutes, most jobs on GitHub-hosted runners did not start within five minutes. Impact eased as we failed over to healthy regions and added capacity. Self-hosted runners were not affected. GitHub Pages sites that build with actions were slow to update, though existing sites continued to serve normally. Some customers also saw errors in repository lists, licensing and billing pages, and some Copilot features.

Actions jobs stayed queued or failed to start because the service that assigns jobs to GitHub-hosted runners stopped working reliably. A partial networking failure on our cloud provider’s side disrupted some of the connections between one of our datacenter regions and the cloud-hosted databases that service depends on. Instead of failing fast, the service waited for those calls to time out. The waiting calls piled up until the service ran out of memory and restarted.

Jobs then shifted to the same service in a healthy region, which did not have enough capacity for the extra demand and began failing too. At the same time, runners that went several minutes without receiving a job shut down and were slow to be replaced, so fewer runners were available to pick up jobs.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 minutes of failed or slow requests across github.com, followed by approximately 3 hours and 30 minutes during which enterprise migrations were paused.

Customers may have seen server errors or slow responses when signing in, working with repositories and pull requests, calling the API, or using GitHub Codespaces. Retrying a short time later would have succeeded, and delayed webhook deliveries caught up soon after. At the peak, about 1.3% of all requests failed or timed out, and about 6.4K organizations saw at least one failed or slow request.

Migrations were paused for customers using GitHub Enterprise Importer, and were resumed once a fix was deployed.

A surge in migration activity caused GitHub Enterprise Importer to send a burst of very large queries to a shared database. These queries took much longer than usual and, together with normal traffic, used all of the database’s available connections, preventing other github.com features relying on the same database from completing their requests.

The importer did not reduce its load when the database became overloaded. The impact ended within minutes, once the importer finished its queued queries and the database’s connections were released.

To prevent a recurrence, we paused migrations until we deployed a mitigation that runs these queries in smaller batches.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: two separate write outages lasted approximately 10 minutes and 9 minutes, totaling about 19 minutes. The second was a recurrence of the first, with the same cause.

Customers may have seen errors when pushing code, signing in, updating pull requests or issues, or making changes through the API. Webhooks, GitHub Apps and OAuth, actions, code scanning, codespaces, and Copilot were also affected. Viewing content was largely unaffected. Data that was already saved was not lost, and actions that failed during the outages succeeded when retried after recovery.

Web and API request failures peaked at 8.9% in the first outage and 9.3% in the second, affecting more than 12,000 and more than 11,000 organizations, respectively. Some organizations may have been affected by both outages.

During regular maintenance, we replaced machines that manage where database writes are sent. One new machine started with outdated records that still listed retired database servers. Once it was automatically elected leader, it published routing settings that sent writes for several core databases to those retired servers. Incorrect settings passed our existing validation and took effect immediately. Later, an automated maintenance task did not honor a pause on maintenance and triggered another election, and because the new machine had not yet been removed, it became leader again.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 28 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in GitHub Actions workflow status updates, logs, and checks. About 5% of jobs on GitHub-hosted runners experienced delayed starts, a very small share of workflow runs failed, and some requests to the actions jobs REST API returned errors. GitHub Pages deployments and workflow and check webhook events generated by actions runs were also delayed. For part of this time, live updates on github.com and code search were degraded.

An internal actions service that stores workflow logs and run status lost connections to some of its cache servers in one cloud region. Every server running that service then retried those connections at the same time. Together, those retries saturated the network connections between GitHub’s data center and that region, disrupting other services that use the same link.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Customers may have seen delays in pull request updates, GitHub Actions workflow status updates, and webhook deliveries. After a push, new commits were slow to appear on pull requests. Workflows triggered by the push started late. Status checks from actions workflows could look stuck on pull requests, which held up merges that require those checks to pass. These features recovered within about 2 to 3.5 hours.

Audit log events were affected the longest. Recent activity took longer to appear when customers searched their audit logs, with delays of up to 1 hour and 50 minutes. Audit log events were fully caught up after about 6 hours and 46 minutes.

Some webhook deliveries from this period may be missing from webhook delivery history, though the webhooks themselves were delivered.

Some servers in our event streaming platform were close to their memory limits, and memory use on these servers grows with the number of client connections. When requests to these servers failed, new connections were opened immediately, which increased the number of connections and the memory they used. The increase in memory use slowed down and overloaded the servers.

We took the overloaded servers out of service, and their traffic moved to other servers. Those servers then became overloaded too, and the problem spread to more servers over the following hour. We began rebalancing overloaded partitions onto brokers that had available capacity and this mitigated the issue.

Audit logs took the longest to recover. The service that writes audit log events kept restarting on errors from the platform for more than two hours and fell further behind. Once stabilized, it could only write events at a limited rate, so the backlog took several more hours to clear.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Duration: approximately 1 hour and 32 minutes.

Customers may have seen errors when using several GPT-family models in Copilot. Requests using these models in Copilot Chat in IDEs and on github.com, the Copilot CLI, Copilot code review, and the Copilot coding agent returned errors or did not complete. About one in 10 requests to the affected models failed. Other models continued to work, and choosing another model avoided the errors. Auto model selection reduced the errors by sending some requests to an unaffected model.

Code scanning autofix and code quality, which are built on one specific model without an alternative model to switch to, were affected more heavily.

Copilot reaches these models through an upstream model provider and uses a credential to authenticate with that provider. That credential became invalid, the provider began rejecting our requests as unauthenticated, and our service returned those rejections to clients as authentication errors. Copilot features that use these models send their requests through that provider, so they began failing at the same time.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Customers may have seen some requests to github.com hang for up to about 10 seconds and then fail with a server error. Pull request merges and Git operations over SSH and Git LFS were hit hardest. At the worst point, about 43% of merge attempts failed, compared with about 3.5% of API calls. Issues, GitHub Pages, notifications, and sign-in for GitHub Apps and OAuth apps also saw intermittent errors.

A database connection pool used by many github.com services reached its limit, and for several minutes no connections were available. New requests that needed a connection waited until the connection timeout expired and then failed.

The pool was already running near capacity when some update requests started holding their connections far longer than expected. Each one began writing a change, then ran a separate lookup that could take several seconds, keeping its connection reserved but unused the whole time. With little headroom, those held connections helped tip the pool over.

How are we making incidents like this less likely or less impactful?

Follow our status page for real-time updates on status changes and post-incident recaps. To learn more about what we’re working on, check out the engineering section on the GitHub Blog.

#10099. AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery

SPONSORED POST: As cyberattacks become more sophisticated, organizations need to look beyond prevention and ensure they can recover critical data quickly and reliably

Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences.

For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption?

These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one.

This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise,  establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible.

Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite.

InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery.

The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed.

For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery.

Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions.

Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences.

For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation.

#10098. Build Low-Latency Multilingual Voice Agents: Open Weights & Full Deployment Control with NVIDIA Magpie TTS

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

By the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one users notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

Voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Supporting more languages is only part of the challenge. Developers also need the ability to:

Open models change what's possible on every one of these.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new)

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most important latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

The table above shows Magpie served as the NVIDIA NIM, measured on-prem — the optimized container running on your own GPU. The open Hugging Face checkpoint is the same model and your path for research and fine-tuning; the NIM is the tuned serving stack that produces these production latencies. Both run on hardware you control.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

This release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. Compared to the previous release, Magpie shows reduced character error rates (CER) and higher speaker similarity (SSIM) on several languages, with the clearest gains on French and Spanish:

Source: Magpie TTS Multilingual model card. CER lower is better; SSIM higher is better.

The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

While objective metrics help measure progress, speech quality is ultimately perceptual. You can hear the difference yourself on NVIDIA Build or the Hugging Face demo.

Latency you can measure is useful. Latency you can control is even better.

Open weights give developers capabilities that come from owning the deployment. With Magpie you can:

For enterprises building production voice AI, this control over deployment, performance, and customization is often what matters most.

Voice AI in production is a system of models, not a single one. Magpie TTS is part of the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent Developer Example, a reference implementation showing how purpose-built speech, language, and reasoning models work together as a coordinated system — so you can build always-on voice agents, not just better-sounding speech.

The Nemotron Voice Agent developer example provides an end-to-end reference implementation that developers can clone, customize, and deploy in hours. It includes production patterns for:

Rather than assembling individual components from scratch, developers can start from a complete reference architecture and adapt it to their own applications.

#10097. Attackers Say 'Hello' to a Different Scale of Cloud Attack

Researchers dubbed an attack chain "Greeter" after discovering that attackers deliberately covered their trail by leaving "hello" messages in logs.

What began as an exploratory Shodan search for exposed cloud instances has led to the discovery of a broad-ranging AI infrastructure attack campaign that researchers have christened "Greeter." The campaign, which started life as an organized, multistage, systematic attack across cloud providers, reinforces why defenders need to shift their thinking about cloud security to include a layered model built around network access control, data protection, and identity security.

Era Security researchers kicked off the research when the Shodan search engine revealed open Amazon DynamoDB instances where anyone could download data or delete it entirely. They dug a little deeper and found Flowise, a connected open source GenAI development platform, where users can build AI agents powered by large language models (LLMs).

Roughly 90% of the nearly 3,000 scanned Flowise deployments were running unpatched versions vulnerable to a critical code-injection vulnerability, CVE-2024-58351 — and if the researchers could see it, so could attackers. So, Era Security deployed AI-powered honeypots, mostly on Amazon Web Service (AWS), to catch them in action.

Related:LLMjacking Emerges as Thriving Cybercriminal Enterprise

Honeypot technology is "not like it was before," and attackers don't recognize it's a decoy until they're much further into the environment, according to the Era Security research team. In the past, it took three or fourth months to build a realistic honeypot. Today, it's two hours.

"The most important finding wasn't the exploitation technique itself, but it was what happened after," Naor Talmor, chief technology officer (CTO) at Era Security, tells Dark Reading. What ensued was a repeatable, staged methodology where attackers mapped out privileges and the environment, hunted for credentials, exploited cloud metadata services across multiple providers to escalate access, and then locked in persistence, he explains. Attackers also obfuscated their activity by leaving seemingly benign and fleeting "hello" messages in the logs, making detection much more difficult because it requires team to spend time searching for specific indicators of compromise in the logs. Thus, the researchers gave the campaign the "Greeter" moniker.

The sophisticated techniques and persistence show that Greeter isn't an opportunistic smash-and-grab attack, a script kiddie, or someone who had merely stumbled upon the honeypots, the researchers noted. And, the campaign was deployed across several AWS regions at once, which indicates broader scale and intent.

Related:External Teams Chats Anchor 15-Minute Malware Delivery

Era Security warns of the potential scale the campaign could reach, confirming 46 real-world victims so far, based on the number of unauthenticated instances that mirrored the honeypot conditions. The team estimates that at least 50% of those remain connected to the Internet and visible, suggesting at least 20 organizations are currently exposed. The sophistication levels of the the threat actors also speaks to how how valuable the cloud and AI attack surface has become, given the effort required to launch Greeter; this wasn't low-hanging fruit.

The Greeter campaign signals a few shifts across the cloud landscape, including how much easier it's gotten for attackers to go unnoticed in workflows. Much of that is due to AI, which threat actors are using to assist in writing code or orchestrating attack steps, according to the Greeter attack logs.

A decade ago, cloud attacks targeted the Docker API. Threat actors then began exploiting workloads, escaping containers to reach the cloud's metadata server underneath, and exploiting service accounts from there, the researchers explain. While attackers are following a similar pattern, they are now using AI infrastructure as the new way to establish persistence.

Related:TiDB Breach Exposes Flawed Cloud Security Assumptions

Researchers agree that the end goal on each instance was to grab cloud credentials and perform lateral movement within a targeted organization.

Meanwhile, attribution remains quite challenging. When the researchers drilled down to the code and techniques, they started to see Chinese characters, though that could be a false flag. Still, a nation-state culprit would make since, because the notion of seeing an "entire orchestration, not even a big cybercrime group could execute that," according to Era Security.

The current velocity of vulnerability exploitation is nothing like the researchers have seen in the past, which puts immense pressure on organizations' traditional patching cycles. This played out just over the past few weeks alone, as security teams raced to fix PHP2Shell and OpenSSH, searching workloads one by one for flaws. However, the Greeter campaign shows a defense challenge for cloud security that's bigger than fixing any specific vulnerability.

Everyone needs to assume a breach now, warns Talmor, adding how if it's not a vulnerability, it may be leaked credentials or an exposed API. Organizations need to design security programs around the cloud to be ready for all of the above, he advises, adopting defense-in-depth.

"A lot of companies adopt that, but they don't really practice it," he notes.

The researchers say organizations can detect this kind of attack much faster if teams monitor for enumeration activity to close gaps before attackers find them. When applications or chat tools are installed, logging can be activated and streamed to a separate location so that even if attackers do delete a device's local history, the logs remain stored in the cloud.

Researchers also noted that this should be monitored closely in critical environments, especially where crown jewels or critical applications are involved, adding that organizations can have dozens or hundreds of accounts depending on the size.

"To be clear, we aren't saying, 'Stop caring about misconfigurations or stop caring about vulnerabilities," Talmor says, warning that patch management is a game "we are losing" that requires organizations to secure their environment layer by layer.

Arielle spent the last decade working as a reporter, transitioning from human interest stories to covering all things cybersecurity related in 2020. Now, as a features writer for Dark Reading, she delves into the security problems enterprises face daily, providing context and actionable steps. She looks for stories that go past the initial news to understand where the industry is going. Her coverage areas include identity and access management, cyber risk and operations, industrial control systems, operational technology, and ransomware trends.

She previously lived in Florida where she wrote for the Tampa Bay Times before returning to Boston where her cybersecurity career took off at TechTarget SearchSecurity. When she's not writing about cybersecurity, she pursues personal projects that include a mystery novel and poetry collection.

Discover how we built the open Agent Host Protocol to keep your agent sessions accessible across editors, apps, phones, and the cloud.

Models are now good enough to work for hours or even days on their own. You don’t have to watch over every thing they do, but you still need to be able to check in, no matter where you are. An agent can’t live only inside one application. The work should continue even If you close a window or switch devices.

In GitHub Copilot you can start an agent session in one place and pick it up in another. This session continuity runs on the Agent Host Protocol (AHP), an open standard built first in VS Code and adopted across GitHub. Here’s how it works, what we learned building it, and how you can use it to bring your agents into your own apps and workflows.

GitHub Copilot was first built in VS Code as an extension that bundled its own harness. This gave you access to your agents in VS Code, but it tied their lifetime to the editor. Extensions are attached to a single VS Code window. Close that window, and the agent is gone. Update VS Code, and every agent stops as the application restarts. Connect to a remote machine, and you get an entirely new extension host commit-locked against the version of the VS Code workbench you have.

At the same time, the Copilot app was being developed, alongside the existing GitHub mobile apps for iOS and Android. Each product was doing its own distinct integration with cloud-based agents to work towards delivering session continuity.

Each of these integrations solved the problem for one product, but developers also still want to be able to pull their agents into their own workflows–whether that’s an editor, a terminal, a phone, or a tool they built themselves–and they can’t do that if every client needs its own one-off integration. That’s why developers needed a protocol: a standard, independently versioned language across versions of VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, mobile apps, and any other client that might host an agent. A shared protocol means every client sees the same agents, history, and state without bespoke integrations, and you aren’t tied to one app’s idea of what an agent session is.

The protocol needed to allow multiple clients to interact with the same set of agents seamlessly. Start a session in the cloud from your phone, for example, then continue it from your laptop. It should tolerate network interruptions, reconnections, and concurrent client mutations. And it needed to be full-featured enough for you to do real work from each of your clients.

At the same time, the protocol needed to stay out of agent behavior. Unlike the domains that produced the Language Server Protocol and Debug Adapter Protocol, the world of agents is evolving quickly. That’s why AHP avoids encoding how agents work, and instead focuses on how you want to interact with them.

You also need the protocol to be simple enough to implement on your own client or server. While the full feature set would necessarily be extensive, the core protocol needed to be minimal.

The result of these requirements is the Agent Host Protocol (AHP). It is oriented around URI-identified “channels”, which are the coarsest unit of functionality in the protocol. Every server must implement the root, session, and chat channels, but can also implement more channels that provide terminal support, MCP additions, or OTel reporting, for example.

Within each channel is a reducer-based state object, which drives most of the logic for clients. The server is the arbiter of the state, and each client sends a sequence of actions that either mutate the state or trigger side effects, like sending a chat message. This provides a few very nice properties. Reconnection and replay in poor network conditions are easy: a client sends all queued actions, presents the right ‘loading’ state, and waits for the server to reconcile and acknowledge the actions before confirming them. Clients and servers are straightforward to debug. And reducer-based state also plays nicely with popular UI frameworks like React.

Adopting the Agent Host Protocol in VS Code required building a new harness and agentic stack underneath it. The Copilot Chat extension, which used to provide all of VS Code’s AI and agentic capabilities, had been growing for over three years, reaching over 400,000 lines of TypeScript, not counting tests. But, as a VS Code extension, it was structured around the lifecycle of a VS Code window and depended entirely on the VS Code extension API. Neither that lifetime nor those APIs would be available in a standalone agent host process.

As we started building the Agent Host Protocol in early 2026, the Copilot SDK was also being developed, and it made sense to leverage it as the foundation for the new agentic stack. This was a big transition. It’s easy to build a harness implementation that says hello and can edit files—we were using the agent host to develop the agent host after the first couple weeks—but it’s another thing to build one that covers the long tail of features developers had come to expect from Copilot Chat.

GitHub has had Copilot cloud agents for a couple of years, allowing developers to run tasks in the cloud from any device. While VS Code was quietly developing the Agent Host Protocol, GitHub was looking to expand that capability to coordinate sessions running on your own devices via the Copilot app, or in cloud sandboxes. This was exactly the N:M problem that AHP was built to solve, so adopting the same technology made perfect sense.

From the outset, the GitHub Agent Host had different requirements than VS Code’s implementation. VS Code runs the host locally and can drop its host on other compute over SSH, containers, WSL, or Dev Tunnels, and it is actually included as part of the VS Code Server bundle. The GitHub Agent Host needed to run in the cloud and across a much wider variety of infrastructure, environments, and security constraints.

Those differing requirements are why they’re separate implementations written in different languages: VS Code’s in TypeScript and GitHub’s in Rust. For now, having two agent hosts has been a good acid-test for the protocol itself. How well does it work when two entirely different teams and sets of agents implement the same protocol independently?

Pretty well, it turns out. Like MCP, the Agent Host Protocol provides escape hatches via custom methods and _metadata on objects that consumers can use for out-of-band signaling. After several months heads-down on our respective implementations, our first task as we worked toward unification was inventorying the ways each implementation had extended the protocol. Many of these extensions reasonably stay GitHub-specific, such as the GitHub Agent Host using metadata to link to project boards. In other cases, variance was a sign of a gap in the protocol; early versions, for example, could not accurately represent shell-type tool output that wasn’t backed by a PTY. And some were bad assumptions, like VS Code’s client assuming a particular structure for the session URIs it received from the agent host. A protocol with only one implementation isn’t truly portable; as we taught our clients and servers to talk to each other, AHP became portable in practice, not just in theory.

Today, the Agent Host Protocol provides that same continuity across all VS Code and GitHub surfaces. Agent sessions running locally in the GitHub Copilot app, in cloud sandboxes, and in VS Code all share the same underlying protocol. To see how it’s used, read about how you can work from anywhere with the new connected Copilot cloud experience.

AHP was designed to be easy to use in clients and servers. Agent Host Protocol libraries are available in Rust, TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift, .NET, and Go, and agents are able to build clients and servers with little prompting. I have a macropad sitting on my desk that reflects my agent’s state in real time, and others have built everything from smart watch apps to Kanban-style task management tools against the protocol. Whether you want a companion app for your own agents, a way to bring agent sessions into your team’s tools, or AHP support in your own editor or agent, the protocol is open for you to build on.

You can connect to an agent host you implement in the Copilot app (enable Experimental > Direct Connections, then go to Environments > Add Agent Host Protocol Host) and in VS Code (via Add Remote Agent Host in the Agents window). You can spawn a standalone version of VS Code’s agent host by running code agent host in your terminal, or see the endpoints for the one in your editor by running code agent endpoints, and samples can help you and your agent get started.

The Agent Host Protocol is an open standard, and questions and suggestions are welcome on GitHub.

Explore the Agent Host Protocol on GitHub >

Agent skills capture repeatable engineering work in files teams can review and reuse, while tools, project context, and permissions remain specific to the host that runs them.

Writing code got faster. The work around it didn’t. See how you can plan, write code, review changes, and investigate production issues with GitHub Copilot, and what work still needs your judgment.

#10095. PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road

Next OS release will bundle modern successor, giving admins a compatibility checklist to work through

Microsoft has confirmed that, at long last, PowerShell 7 will come bundled with Windows, while the venerable PowerShell 5.1 begins its long retirement.

It has been a long time coming, although PowerShell 5.1 isn't going away immediately. It will, however, "be removed from a future version of Windows," and Windows Server 2025 and Windows 11 26H2 are the last versions to include PowerShell 5.1 enabled by default.

After that, PowerShell 5.1 will be available as a Feature On Demand (FOD) before eventually shuffling off into the sunset, while PowerShell 7 takes over automation duties.

PowerShell 5.1 is now more than ten years old and runs on the .NET Framework. PowerShell 7 is its cross-platform, open source successor, but compatibility isn't seamless.

PowerShell was the brainchild of Jeffrey Snover, who sought to bring script automation to Windows at a time when graphical user interfaces were king. He recalled executives telling him "admins don't want command line interfaces," and "exactly what part of effing Windows is confusing you?" but eventually won the argument, and we reckon countless Windows administrators owe him a debt of gratitude.

PowerShell 5.1 hasn't had many new features for years. "PowerShell 7 is the modern PowerShell: the one we develop in the open, across platforms, and where new features go," wrote Jason Helmick, a senior product manager on Microsoft's PowerShell team. But compatibility niggles remain.

The two can run side by side, so existing scripts won't have to move immediately. Finding and testing everything scattered across an enterprise estate, however, could keep administrators occupied for some time.

Microsoft also has unfinished work on the bundled version's MSIX packaging, including support for running as SYSTEM, DISM cmdlets, and machine-wide settings. Those gaps matter for scheduled tasks, services, and management scripts.

Despite the deprecation, PowerShell 5.1 will continue to receive updates based on the lifecycle of the Windows version on which it runs. It will eventually be removed based on usage data and "communicated in advance," according to Microsoft.

Administrators have time to prepare, but checking which scripts run unchanged, which need work, and which still depend on 5.1 won't happen by itself.

"Including PowerShell 7 in Windows is a milestone we've been working toward since PowerShell went cross-platform," Helmick wrote, although the bundled release is still ahead.

Microsoft says PowerShell 7 will arrive with the next Windows release, but hasn't named it. 27H2, anyone? ®
